Mr. Diefenbaker refused to consult with his own party, or to consider any reasonable compromise himself.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the house I should like to table a copy of a letter dated August 25 which I have received from the charge d'affaires of Japan informing me of the voluntary restraints which the Japanese government is applying on the export of certain products to Canada during 1964. These decisions were taken by the Japanese government following consultations which began in December, 1963 between the Japanese and Canadian governments. The levels of restraint which Japan is maintaining during 1964 provide generally for orderly increases over the 1963 levels. These increases are in the order of 3 per cent to 5

per cent, and in virtually all cases these increases are not greater than the expected growth in the market for the products in question.
By leave of the house I suggest that the charge's letter be printed as an appendix to Hansard in view of the interest it has for a large number of people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: VOLUNTARY RESTRAINTS ON EXPORTS TO CANADA
speechtext:
I would like to take this opportunity to express appreciation for the cooperation shown by the Japanese government in the working out of these arrangements. The discussions have, of course, been long and difficult. We would not expect them to be otherwise, since they affect important sectors of Japanese trade just as they relate to important and sensitive sectors of the Canadian economy.
It might be useful if I reminded the house that last year during the course of consultations the Canadian government agreed to the removal of vinyl raincoats from the list of items under restraint by Japan. Following our policy of not seeking restraints on exports when damage to Canadian producers is no longer threatened, we agreed this year that plywood might be removed from the list of items under restraint.
It might also be useful if I said a word about our discussions with Japan on exports of worsted fabrics. There has been some speculation in the press on this subject and, accordingly, I would like to report briefly on where this matter now stands.
In late 1963 representations were received on behalf of Canadian producers of worsteds asking that Japan be asked to restrain exports. These representations were examined closely; it was apparent that until that time the very sharp increase in imports from Japan had been largely at the expense of other supplying countries, and had not directly affected Canadian producers. It was evident, however, that if imports from Japan continued to grow at that rate Canadian producers would soon be threatened with material injury. Japanese exports of worsteds to Canada in 1963 rose by 60 per cent over 1962. The statistics so far available indicate that

imports of worsteds from Japan this year may be up by a further 50 per cent or 60 per cent over 1963. This would represent a total value of imports of Japanese worsteds far in excess of Japanese exports of worsteds to all of Europe last year.
It is important to note that Japanese exports of worsteds to virtually every industrial market except Canada and the United States are strictly controlled, either in Japan or in the importing country. This means that exports from Japan will tend to be concentrated on the relatively open Canadian market.
While we have had a number of discussions with the Japanese, no agreement has so far been reached on how to deal with this problem or the level of restraint that might be warranted. I will be taking this matter up further with Japanese ministers at the meeting in Tokyo next week, and I am still hopeful that some understanding on worsted fabrics will be reached which will meet the legitimate interests of all parties concerned, including the Canadian producers, the Japanese exporters and the Canadian users of Japanese goods.

maintopic: VOLUNTARY RESTRAINTS ON EXPORTS TO CANADA
speechtext:
I understand the finalization of these matters will take place in further meetings in Tokyo next week. But the minister said, I believe, in the early part of his remarks that the expected increase in quotas would about balance the increase in the requirements of this country. This, it seems to me, leaves a somewhat narrow margin for any increase in production in Canada and for the increased consumption in Canada of Canadian products.
It has been reported that there has been a worsening of our deficit position, or that there has been a big increase in our imports and a drop in exports; also in regard to the United States there has been a decrease in exports and an increase in imports amounting to 6.9 per cent. I wonder whether the minister is keeping this over-all picture in mind as he looks forward to further increases in imports of goods from Japan. I wonder whether he does not feel this situation is worthy of serious consideration.

maintopic: VOLUNTARY RESTRAINTS ON EXPORTS TO CANADA
speechtext:
When we have had a chance to examine this list of voluntary restraints on Japanese imports into Canada we shall be in a better position to make a statement regarding it.
However, I think the house should remember-and I am sure the government is aware of this fact-that Japan is still buying from us a great deal more than we are buying from

her. Trade is a two way street, and if Japan and other countries are to buy from Canada they can only do so if they are able to earn Canadian dollars with which to pay for these goods. I think this must be kept in mind when we examine these voluntary restrictions. We shall be glad, in this party, to consider this list and make a statement at an appropriate time.

maintopic: VOLUNTARY RESTRAINTS ON EXPORTS TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we listened with interest, of course, to the statement just made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) on trade and financial arrangements made or to be made with Japan. However, in this connection one thing in particular should be borne in mind, and it is this. Even if our trade balance with Japan is favourable we should not forget that the labour content in the goods we import from Japan is much higher than the labour content in the goods we export to Japan. As a matter of fact, our exports to Japan consist mostly of raw materials with, unfortunately, a very small Canadian labour content, so that, as an end result, we are still showing a deficit as far as labour is concerned.
The same thing can be said about our trade with other countries; that is the problem we are now facing and will continue to face unless we change our policy as far as international trade is concerned.

maintopic: VOLUNTARY RESTRAINTS ON EXPORTS TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only a few words to say about the statement just made by the Minister of Finance. According to the minister we have a favourable trade balance with Japan since they import more from us than we do from them.
Now, some Canadian associations have complained to the Minister of Finance against some sort of dumping by Japan in Canada. Consequently, I feel the minister is not quite right in saying that after investigating the situation he is satisfied that such dumping does no harm to Canadian trade and industry.
As he knows, there are Canadian and American companies in Japan at present. As the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) said a moment ago, our raw material is exported to Japan where it is cheaper to process it, and then it is exported back to Canada. Those are our imports. Let no one tell us that our trade and industry do not suffer from the fact that Canadians settle in Japan instead of producing what we need right here in Canada.
Questions
We live in an era when it is absolutely necessary to do business with the other nations of the world, but not to the disadvantage of Canada or other nations. That our international trade should balance, that is in order. However, let no one tell us that goods which enter Canada from Japan and which could be produced here in Canada do not hurt Canadian industry. If Canadians expatriate themselves and settle in Japan because labour is cheaper, the necessary action should be taken to encourage production and industry in Canada so that we may have more and more control over our general economy as well as over imports and exports which concern us.

subtopic: TELEGRAMS DEMANDING RESIGNATION OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS MINISTER
speechtext:
Order. We started the question period at 2.25 and by virtue of the

recent standing order, temporary if you wish,
the half hour period ended at 2.57. It is now
just three o'clock.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, August 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.
And the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. More.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking at this time on the subamendment I think I would be remiss if I did not say a word or two in commendation of my colleagues for the many outstanding and patriotic addresses they have made in the house, and I think you will put up with me for a moment when I say many of us were so pleased last night that the hon. member for Huron made such an outstanding address. I believe he is the oldest member of the house in terms of age and the second oldest member of the house in terms of years of service.
I have no intention of speaking on the flag, but I do intend to speak on the subamendment which was moved by the hon. member for Regina City on August 13, and which is recorded at page 6806 of Hansard for that date. I think it would be only proper for us to refresh our minds by taking another look at the question he proposed at that time. The first one was, "Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign?" The second was, "Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign with changes made thereon to show the main heritage of both founding races?" The third was, "Are you in favour of the three maple leaf design?"
Hear, hear.

The fourth was "Are you in favour of a one maple leaf design?" I appreciate, Mr. Speaker, the action of hon. members on the other side in putting punctuation marks at the end of each of those sentences.
I think this proposal would give every Canadian an opportunity to exercise his freedom of choice, an opportunity to express his
Canadian Flag
opinion as to what we should have by way of a national flag. It was my privilege to address the house on July 2, at which time I spoke at great length on the subject of the flag. As a result I have received many letters. I have a file here which any member who wishes may examine; it contains some 200 or 300 letters on this subject sent to me between the date of that address and today. These letters are not all from people with Anglo-Saxon names, though there are, of course, a large number which bear such names. There are also a great many letters from people whose names indicate a French background. Then again, a great many of the names suggest a background which is neither Anglo-Saxon nor French. For example, I have had letters from people with names such as Steve Marti, G. W. Snetsinger, Mike Hillcoff, J. Melkonian, Janet Schaef, A. C. Petrouski, Dr. H. C. Soltan and Zudy Martinovic. I could mention further names, but one which comes to my mind immediately, because it is a name which was borne by a man who rendered signal service to this house, is the name Aberhart. So these people do not all come from one national background.
Many of these letters are interesting. I do not intend to read them all, and I know hon. members will be happy about that. At the same time I must direct the attention of the house to some of them. I have letters from as far away as Manitoba. Many are from Quebec. There are some from New York state, some from Michigan and one from a correspondent in England. Among all these letters there is only one in support of the proposed new flag, and I am thankful to say it did not come from within my riding. As I say, one of these letters came from England, and I should like to quote a small portion of it:
I was shocked to read recently In one of the daily papers here in England, that Canada was to have a new flag. A few days ago, I received a letter with a strange stamp on it, but it was a Canadian stamp. The sender of the letter informed me that the design of the stamp was that of the proposed new Canadian flag, which, the writer thought, was to become legal the following week.
As one of your supporters I am writing to protest very strongly against the proposed new flag.
I have another letter which came to me as recently as yesterday. I should like to quote a portion of it because I think it is important and would make a contribution to this debate. It comes from the city of London under date of August 21, and it says:
I did want to say thank you for your recent copy of 'House of Commons Debates' with the particular reference to your part played in this tremendous issue of the national flag.

Canadian Flag
I want to express my appreciation of the way in which the Conservative party have fought this issue. I cannot help but feel very proud of all that has transpired upon the floor of the house, not unmindful of the many hours the honourable members must have spent in meetings, sittings, etc.
It has been a very grave and grim summer for .all concerned, but little do we realize, so far from the actual scene of action, how wearying and, at times, discouraging, this all can be to the human mind and body.
Once again, my sincere thanks for a job well done. Whatever the outcome, whatever flag flies as our official national flag in the days to come, the Conservative party of Canada can well remember with honour this glorious summer of 1964.
Hear, hear.

It is apparent that the words which have come from this House of Commons and gone out across the country are making an impression upon the people of this great nation of ours.
I should like to quote now from an article which was published in the London Free Press under date of May 23, 1964. It was written by Mr. Arthur R. Ford, who is editor emeritus of our paper in London. It is headed "Will New Flag Provide Unity?"
For my part I think it is a mistake nationally for a minority government to press this issue. Personally I think it will divide the country more than ever. I have a high regard for Mr. Pearson, for his achievements in his career as a Canadian diplomat. He has raised the status of Canada at the United Nations and in the international world.
Mr. Pearson, however, is asking a lot from Canadians of British or U.E. Loyalist stock to pull down the union jack, although most of us will accept it if it will put an end to the movement in Quebec for separatism, associate states and terrorism and bring about national unity, but I doubt whether the new flag or the new anthem will satisfy the Quebec extremists.
Most people in this part of Canada are prepared to go far, and to lean backwards, to meet fair and reasonable demands of French Canada. They earnestly want to join with them in building a greater Canada. They realize that the old Quebec is disappearing and that a new and modern [DOT]Quebec is rising. The University of Western Ontario, a number of years ago, led the way by establishing a summer school at Trois Pistoles to give students of the university an opportunity, not only to learn French, but to understand French Canada. In recent years there has been a movement in the schools to broaden the use of French.
There are certain principles, however, which they are not prepard to surrender. They want a continuation of the connection with Great Britain, through a common membership in the commonwealth of nations. They want to retain the monarchy with the Queen of Great Britain also the Queen of Canada. They want a retention of the British parliamentary system of government, which stands for the possession of those precious freedoms which we have long cherished-the freedom of speech, the freedom of the press, the freedom of association, the freedom of religion and .equal justice.

This is part of an article which was written by one of Canada's most outstanding writers, and I know it came directly from his heart.
Some time ago the Prime Minister said in this house, at the beginning of the flag debate, that everyone would have an opportunity to speak. In fact he urged that all members should get up and express themselves, and I believe it is the right and duty of every member to stand up and express himself on behalf of his constituents. This cannot be considered a filibuster. We received an invitation from the Prime Minister himself to stand up and speak on behalf of our constituents.
On May 25, in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Peace River, we were given to understand that the debate would proceed without interruption and that every member would have a chance to speak. This can be seen by turning to page 3533 of Hansard. Now there is talk of limiting the debate to one week in which to decide something of great national importance whose results we shall have to live with for many years to come. As late as yesterday the Prime Minister made a statement in this chamber in answer to a question. He said:
I still think we should proceed along the course already indicated, and I do not like to think that there is total irreconcilability between positions.
But by his very words, Mr. Speaker, he did admit that there was division. These are some of the things to which I think we should be giving serious thought now. We know there is great division throughout this entire country, perhaps more division than we have ever had in our whole history.
I know the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre referred last night to the article in the Toronto Telegram of August 22, 1964. He quoted one part of it. As a result of his quotation I went through this article, and I believe there are two or three more points that should be brought to the attention of this house and I hope ultimately to the attention of the people throughout this great country of which we are privileged to be citizens. This article goes on to say that the vote cannot be free. It says it is impossible for a vote to be free under these circumstances. Then the article says:
At this stage, with party lines hardened, it is difficult to conceive of a truly free vote.
Having shown, belatedly, a willingness to retreat from his earlier stubborn demands for the banner of his choice, he now should go one step further and measure public sentiment by plebiscite.
Perhaps Mr. Pearson fears the outcome of such a testing of public opinion. Letters and petitions

expressing determination to retain the ensign have been impressive.
There is no reason why this obstructive and divisive bill should not be shelved pending a reference to the people. There is no urgency. Most Canadians outside Quebec appear to be quite satisfied with the flag we have now. In Quebec, the matter is of little importance as there they fly the Laurentian flag with its white cross and fleurs-de-lis.
Until Mr. Pearson softens his stand, the opposition is justified in continuing a modified filibuster.
Regardless of what they may call it, they say they feel we are justified in the stand we have taken; and I think this is the general opinion of Canadians across this country.
Hear, hear.

This article continues:
As distasteful as such devices are in parliament, no other method seems practical in the face of Mr. Pearson's stubbornness.
The way out of the parliamentary impasse is clear; a plebiscite to end the long debate and to allow parliament to get on with more important legislation.
This is the way the people across this country of ours are feeling. I would admit that perhaps three or four weeks ago there was a slightly different feeling; but today, with the number of letters I am receiving in my office and the number of letters I know many other hon. members are receiving, the general idea is "Don't give up the ship. Keep fighting. You are doing a good job". I received word just the other day that the city of London has recently ordered its flag requirements for the next five years. The flag they ordered was the Canadian red ensign.
We could go on at great length, Mr. Speaker, to test the pulse of the people of Canada at the present moment. In the Ottawa Citizen of August 22, last Saturday, there appeared an article on the subject of the flag. I would like to quote one small paragraph that says:
And if the Prime Minister is retreating from the three-leaf flag, the three-leaf flag would appear to have little chance of ever being run up the parliamentary flagpole.
What weakened Mr. Pearson's position?
Further down it says this:
The red ensign is now stronger than ever.
If not above the battle, it at least flew over the battlefield-and its position seems considerably stronger at summer's end than it was at the beginning.
Mr. Pearson is ready to throw the design of a new flag back into committee-a far cry from hopes that it would be flying by July 1, or for the royal visit in October.
Then we have the Ottawa Journal of August 20, last Thursday. I could go on at great length with these quotations, Mr. Canadian Flag
Speaker. Many quotations have been given to the house, but these quotations have not been referred to. In this article appearing in the Ottawa Journal it says-and this shows the difficulty that is confronting the Liberal front benchers-
When the caucus met Tuesday, the Prime Minister missed the assault by the backbench on the cabinet because he was chairing that conclave of the party leaders seeking the elusive negotiated peace in the flag war.
There is an indication that the apple in the bottom of the barrel has gone bad; and we know what happens to the whole barrel as the result of something like that. I know many hon. members of this house have read these articles, and some hon. members on the other side of the house must be very much concerned about this whole question. The feeling is there, and that feeling is growing day by day. And we talk about a free vote. How could there possibly be a free vote? Many hon. members on the other side of the house have already declared their intentions; they have gone to the point where they just cannot go back. In some cases they have told their constituents how they stand. I know, from speaking with some of them personally, that they would like to make an about face now, but how can they do it?
What about the Secretary of State for External Affairs? I think he has passed the point of no return. A recent public opinion poll carried on in Windsor indicated a majority support for the red ensign. What will the minister do now? What is going to happen to him? It is not that I am too concerned personally, but as a minister he may be bound to the Pearson pennant alliance to a point from which he cannot retreat. Which way will he jump? We know he is pretty adept at jumping, but we do not know which way he is going to jump. I'll bet he is somewhat concerned at the moment.
Some of the other things that have come out in the way of propaganda sometimes make one wonder why we do not have a minister of propaganda in this house. They talk about the cost of keeping the house open. I believe that recently-I may be wrong, and if I am I stand to be corrected-the secretarial staff were told they would be employed throughout any recess we might have. Every member gets his pay whether he is here or not. What is the expense of keeping this house open? We have many visitors here in the summer; we have to keep it open for them to come in. Perhaps there is the cost of printing Hansard, Votes and Proceedings and things of that type. But we have no

Canadian Flag
business before the house at the present time, and the time we are now taking, as good Canadians is for the purpose of standing up in this house and fighting for these things we think are right. We are using our holiday time, or our recess time, for that purpose.
Hear, hear.

It is interesting to hear the questions across the floor of this house. I am not too sure that the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition may not be perhaps a little closer to a compromise than we all expect. Wouldn't it be nice if, as Canadians, we could just sit down together and work this thing out and come to a solution that would be satisfactory to everybody? But we cannot do it that way. The only recourse we have is a plebiscite.
I say these things, Mr. Speaker, as a member seeking only to further unity, national unity. It is my hope that they will come together and in some way establish an allparty committee which would select a flag which would be of truly non-partisan design.
The subject which is before us is the subamendment. It is my opinion that we should have a plebiscite, Mr. Speaker. However, let me go a little further and ask: Should we have a plebiscite now? To this question I would answer no. I would say, let us file away until the next election, which may not be too far off, this whole contentious issue, which is upsetting the country and causing so much division among the people. Then at that time let us have a plebiscite on this matter. If we were to have a plebiscite now we would have to put the whole of our election machinery into action. Through enumerators, we would have to prepare voters lists and employ all those people and services which are necessary in order to hold a plebiscite. This would cost just about as much as a general election and would be a waste of $15 million. There is no reason why this matter cannot be filed away and left aside until such time as we have an election. Then we could have the plebiscite, whether it be in November or March or a year hence. In the meantime let us get together as good Canadians should, and make sure that this parliament works in the best interests of the people in the Dominion of Canada. In this way we can kill two birds with one stone as well as save ourselves some money.
By approaching the subject in this way we will provide three opportunities to the people of Canada. First of all, we will give them a chance to simmer down and think about the matter a little less passionately

than they are thinking about it at the moment. It would give them an opportunity to think clearly. The people are mad, and they are mad because they may be losing their red ensign. They are mad about that, and the great waves of protest are growing daily. We are not afraid of having a plebiscite because we know what the answer will be.
In addition, we will save $15 million. I think it was the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) who said "What's a hundred million?", and we know he was being facetious. But $15 million is a lot of money, and we should have it if we can.
The most important thing we shall be giving the people is this. We will be giving them the opportunity of exercising their freedom of choice. We cannot let down now. We must carry on. The only alternative for us if we bow down and accept the flag which has been presented by one person is, in essence, to let the people of the country down and give in to what is almost a virtual dictatorship.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to participate in this debate for the second time. I do so only because the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), for one, made in my opinion a rather provocative speech and I thought it only appropriate to answer him today. Second, the subamendment before us should be given serious consideration by the government. It is quite obvious that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is not interested in considering anything but the original or initial resolution, but it is with the hope that he will reconsider the matter that I take part once more in this debate. I also want to deal with some of the recommendations made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) whose speech a few days ago could well be considered one of the better ones delivered in this house for a long time.
I might just say that I am very interested to see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays), a fellow Albertan from the city of Calgary, in his seat today. I welcome him back. It is of course my hope that he will participate in this debate during the course of this afternoon because I know how some of the people of Calgary feel about this question. I should also like to know how the minister himself feels. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, it appears at the moment as if our country is getting along on its own in spite of parliament rather than because of it. Again I plead with the Prime Minister to give this matter serious consideration, or if you like reconsideration.

When one looks at the subamendment introduced by the hon. member lor Regina City (Mr. More) he finds it poses four questions, namely: Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign? Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign modified? Are you in favour of the three maple leaves design? Are you in favour of a one maple leaf design? What possible objection could the Prime Minister see to a plebiscite on this question during some future election? What he would in fact be doing is allowing those people, and there are many of them, who have not communicated with their members of parliament either by petition or letter or telephone, and who feel strongly with respect to the questions involved in the subamendment, to express their viewpoints on the subject. What is more fair, Mr. Speaker, than to give these people the opportunity to mark an X against the appropriate question during an election? It would then give the red ensigners the opportunity to express their point of view. It would give those who feel strongly about the red ensign but would be quite willing to accept a slight modification to express their point of view. Then again it would allow those who are in favour of either one of the two other designs to express their point of view as well. What could be more fair than that, Mr. Speaker? I do not understand the Prime Minister's reticence with regard to action on this matter.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle suggested, as an alternative: Why not refer the matter to a parliamentary committee? Although I think this would be my second preference, I see nothing wrong with turning the question over to a parliamentary committee composed of an equal number of members from the two largest parties in the House of Commons, and members from the other parties in the house.
I suggest there are approximately 3,500 designs in the possession of the government at the moment. Surely the committee could study these designs, select half a dozen and then unanimously decide on one design out of the half dozen they have chosen from the 3,500. If it is insisted that a time limit should be imposed on the committee, then I say that to my mind this is not workable and will not work. I think the committee should be instructed to sit for a given number of days, and it might be a year or two years before a final report is received by the house. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) laughs. I think this is a very reasonable alternative to what the Prime Minister has proposed. Hon. members know what his proposal is. He proposes to shove it down people's throats.

Why not ten years?
I did not hear the comment.
Why not ten years?

I see nothing wrong with ten years if that is how long it takes the committee to decide. At least there would be one consolation. The people of Canada would be united when a final decision was made. You will not unite this country by forcing a flag down the throats of the Canadian people.
Let us talk about the resolution. I have more regard for relevancy than the Minister of Trade and Commerce had when he spoke on this subject, and it is my hope that when the Minister of Agriculture rises to participate in the debate he will also be relevant. Since the introduction of the resolution letters have been written to members of parliament including the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), the Prime Minister (Mr.. Pearson) and all the cabinet ministers. Polls have been conducted by various groups, organizations and newspapers. Petitions have been signed with thousands of signatures on them. Some have been sent to the Prime Minister and some to the respective members of parliament. On many occasions inside and outside the House of Commons speeches have been made on the merits, pros and cons of a flag.
I want to deal with some of the polls that have been conducted throughout the country since the resolution was introduced. I might point out, Mr. Speaker, and you will probably find it as interesting as I do, that in one recent survey conducted by a well known international magazine the city of Edmonton had the greatest percentage per 1,000 telephone calls in support of the red ensign of any city in Canada. Edmonton is a cosmopolitan city like Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver, and the suggestion that certain ethnic groups, people of certain racial backgrounds, support or do not support either of the flag proposals before the house is wrong. People generally in the city of Edmonton, and I know this applies to Calgary also, are predominantly red ensign supporters.
I refer now to a survey that was conducted by the Edmonton Journal early in May of this year. The Journal polled residents of the city of Edmonton and district on whether or not they were in favour of the red ensign and after about a week these were the results. A total of 1,636 ballots were cast in favour of the red ensign compared with 862 in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag, and

Canadian Flag
a large number of people simply said it did not matter to them at all.
Would the hon. member give us the question that was asked?
I will be very glad to deal with that.
Carried.

I am still on my feet, Mr. Speaker. For the benefit of the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Godin) I am trying to find the question that was asked in the poll but I do not seem to have it in front of me at the moment.

I asked that question because from the remarks of the hon. member I understood that the question was, "Are you in favour of the red ensign". In my opinion that question alone would not elicit the type of answer that would give a proper indication of the opinion of the people.
I have just arranged to have my office called-
Mr. Speaker, it is not-

Order. The hon.
member for Edmonton East has the floor.
I know that the hon. member for Nickel Belt is jealous. He wants to support the Prime Minister whether he is right or wrong, and I do not blame him for inquiring-

On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I do not think any member should refer to another member of the house as doing something, right or wrong, on the basis of partiality. I have had occasion to make a speech in the house on this matter-
Mr. Speaker-
Order. The hon. member for Nickel Belt is rising on a question of privilege and perhaps the hon. member for Edmonton East will give him an opportunity to state his point.

Mr. Speaker, I was drawing the attention of the house to the fact that no member of parliament should indicate that another member is doing something on the basis of partiality, which was the intent of the remarks of the hon. member. I had occasion to make a speech in the house on the matter of the flag and it is unfortunate that the hon. member was not present to hear it.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has muddied up his question of privilege so that now no one understands it.

I did not accuse the hon. and learned gentleman of being right or wrong with respect to the resolution. I said he was supporting the Prime Minister and he did not care whether the Prime Minister was right or wrong. I did not accuse the hon. member of doing anything-

On the question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I insist that the remarks of the hon. member indicate that some members of this house-it happens to be me on this occasion-are doing something on the basis of partiality. The hon. member says that no matter if the Prime Minister is right or wrong I will support him. I support the Prime Minister because what he has done is good for Canada.
Mr. Speaker, this is precisely-

Order. I can understand the feelings of the hon. member for Nickel Belt but I really do not think it is unparliamentary to suggest that an hon. member is either voting or speaking because of partiality. I would suspect that many speeches made in the house are inspired by that feeling. I do not really think the hon. member has said anything up to now that is unparliamentary and should be withdrawn.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I feel very badly that the hon. member should consider my remarks offensive. I understand his blind desire to defend the Prime Minister's actions, whether he is right or wrong. I say that he is wrong and I intend to prove that before I conclude my remarks, if the hon. member will permit me to continue.
As I pointed out, the Edmonton Journal conducted a survey by ballot, and the ballots will be delivered to my desk in a few minutes, I hope. The readers were asked to sign their ballots as evidence of their good faith, but the names would not be recorded on the ballots themselves, which would go forward to a distant point for tabulating. The results would be published as the reports were compiled. I have already put some of the reports on the record, Mr. Speaker. I was more than amazed that the city of Edmonton would respond so overwhelmingly in support of the ensign.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

I would grant the hon. member that courtesy if he would promise me he would get up and make a speech on the

flag issue after I have listened to his question.

It seems to me it is the privilege of this house, if an hon. member purports to give evidence which will convince any hon. member of this house of one thing or another, to ask the hon. member to inform the house properly of the facts behind the evidence he is producing. This is what hon. members are now asking. We should have the privilege of knowing the facts behind the evidence which he is producing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not believe the point of order or question of privilege is well taken. It seems to me this is a question of debate. If the hon. member feels the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Edmonton East cannot be substantiated, he can say so in reply to the speech made by the hon. member.

I rise on a question of privilege. I would call Your Honour's attention to the wording of the statement on the prior question of privilege. The hon. member used the words, "if the member has any evidence to convince any member in this chamber". The hon. member has evidence that will convince me and many members on this side, therefore his statement in reference to any member does not hold water and there is no question of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We cannot permit a debate on the point.

As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, the results of the survey taken by the Edmonton Journal were indeed impressive. A month or two after the original survey in May, another survey was taken. By this time the article to which I am referring, dated June 26, had been written. It is entitled "Two out of three favour red ensign" and deals with the question on a national basis, with the exception of the province of Quebec. I should like to read one paragraph from this news article because I think hon. members from the city of Toronto would find it very interesting indeed. Before I do, I may say that the city of Edmonton survey shows that two of three Journal readers favour the red ensign as Canada's national flag. Toronto has plumped most heavily for the ensign, with Telegram readers casting 7,865 ballots for it and 1,839 for the Pearson flag. I am just wondering how the members from the city of Toronto, 18 of them in all, feel when they sit on their hands in the House of Commons without expressing a point of view.

One did.

Yes, and I dare say hon. members across the house wish he had never opened his mouth.
There is another comment in an Ottawa report by Patrick Nicholson dated August 21, a few days ago. I am still dealing with the poll that was started originally in the city of Edmonton by the Edmonton Journal. This article says:
It quickly became obvious that "Mike's maple" had attracted overwhelming support among French Canadians, while the lukewarm enthusiasm for it elsewhere was gravely tempered by the resentment, as some M.P.'s expressed it, that this was "yet another concession to French Canada".
I want to deal with the aspect of this remark because, as a political party, we have been accused of using the words "massive concessions". I want to assure you that of all the speeches I have read, one man used those words and used them deliberately, and that was the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp).
I continue to quote from the article:
The lopsidedness of cross-Canada sentiment on the flag issue has just been revealed by a nationwide poll, whose sensational results were given front page prominence in Ottawa's thoughtful French language newspaper, Le Droit.
This poll discovered that a majority of Canadians, in every province except Quebec, prefer the Canadian ensign to the maple leaf design. It also ascertained that about one third of all Canadians would prefer some other flag, such as the union jack or another design, or were ignorant or indifferent about the whole issue.
The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Godin) looks at me as though he were familiar with the article and wished me to quote another paragraph. If he asks me to do so, I will.
I would prefer to hear your views.

Why will the Prime Minister not consider the modification of the red ensign? Why will he not consider an alternative? I suppose, to be fair, one ought to give him the benefit of the doubt. However, I must ask this pertinent question-

The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Godin) was complaining about this

Neither are his interruptions. These are the four questions I want to ask the Prime Minister: Is he not proud of the union jack? Is this why he wants to get rid of the red ensign, because it has a small union jack in the corner? Is he not proud of it? If he is not, why is he not? How can the Prime Minister justify shoving down the throats of Canadians a flag that does not have a cross on it? These are the three questions I would like to ask the Prime Minister. I talked a moment ago about the pride which Hawaii has in its flag, and in that connection here is an interesting clipping from the Edmonton Journal:
Thousands oi Albertans who have visited Hawaii must have seen widely displayed there a flag incorporating the union jack.
It is, of course, the state flag of Hawaii: a union jack in the upper corner next to the staff and eight vertical stripes, three white, three red and two blue.
What about the subamendment?
Why the hell don't you get up and speak?

I hear a chirp from the backwoods. I cannot identify the member because he will not stand. He has no guts. The article goes on to say:
No nation treats its flag with more reverence than does the United States, and no state is prouder to be part of the U.S. than is Hawaii. Nevertheless, the incorpration of the union jack in the state flag of this "melting pot" of nationalities suggests that Hawaii does not wish to forget the British role in its history.
What was that British role in Hawaii's history? Captain James Cook, the English navigator, discovered the islands in 1778, and if it had not been for the attitude of the British parliament Hawaii would still be a colony or a holding of the British empire. The article goes on to say:
It would be preposterous to charge that Prime Minister Pearson is not proud of the union jack.

I posed that question a moment ago, but I
had very little or no response.
But has he been unduly Influenced by men who irrationally and perversely oppose the incorporation of the union jack in Canada's national flag? Certainly there is no national symbol anywhere that can rightfully evoke greater pride and reverence.
Will the day come when the shortest trip Albertans can take to see the union jack proudly waving in the breeze will be Hawaii?
I ask the Prime Minister, what are his reasons? Is it that as a Britisher himself he dislikes the union jack? Why doesn't the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) get up and answer?
On a point of order, so that the house may understand the meaning of the remarks of the hon. member would he indicate is he suggesting-
I have not yielded the floor.

Mr. Speaker, you have been more than generous in the half hour I have been on my feet. I have been trying to explain to the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Godin), and in very plain common language, what it is I am talking about, and he does not understand. I said I was posing four questions to the Prime Minister. Is he not proud of the union jack? Why should he be ashamed of it? Can he justify stuffing down
Canadian Flag
the throats of Canadians a flag that does not have a cross on it?
In talking about the true meaning of the union jack to people of British ancestry, who have been connected with it for generations, I want to make brief reference to a newspaper article which is headed, "That Leafy Flag Repudiates the Cross," and I shall quote a few short paragraphs from it.
The article is by Frank Chubb, minister of St. Stephen's United church, Edmonton, and I think the quotation will be very relevant indeed. I am quoting it for the benefit of the hon. member who spent the last half hour interrupting me and who has finally left the chamber.
It would be hard to conceive of a greater affront to us as a Christian nation than that of being informed arbitrarily that the cross must be removed from our flag.
I suggest this is precisely what is happening now as a result of an action taken arbitrarily without consultation either in caucus or in cabinet. As I pointed out in the course of my last speech, the article by Val Sears obviously had some significance because of the objections which were raised. This flag design was born over a bottle of scotch and soda. Now I can understand why they want to leave the cross out of it. The article goes on to say:
If it symbolizes anything, the flag represents what the nation stands for. Has the idea of sacrificing for the good of others now become so unpalatable to us as a people that the cross must come out of our flag?
If so, the prospects for our future as a nation have reached an all time low.
These are the views of a minister of an influential religious body in Canada. May I say, for the benefit of hon. members opposite, that I do not intend to quote at length. I just want to put on record one other passage from this article. This is what the writer says about the significance of the cross:
We Canadians had preserved this rich heritage in the comer of the red ensign, the flag adopted by the Canadian government and people in 1945.
Now Mr. Pearson says it must go.
He seems to believe that three leaves off an eastern Canadian tree are more than adequate as a substitute for the three great crosses on our flag.
Along with the crosses must go the coat of arms we requested from His Majesty King George V a scant 43 years ago.
What a tribute to infidelity and fickleness.
Certainly it is time for Canada to take on individuality and responsibility as a nation, but must a child disown its parents in order to achieve healthy maturity?
I should think that the opposite is the case!
The Canadian coat of arms on the red ensign traces our heritage back to 1,100 years before the

Canadian Flag
birth of Christ. A Canadian worth his salt should be able to feel a bit of a thrill as he sees outlined against the sky these symbols of the glory from which he has sprung.
When someone pretending to "lead" the people of Canada suggests that we repudiate the cross and reject our heritage, when all he can offer in return is a handful of leaves, the time is ripe not merely for dissent, but for revolution.
These are strong words. These are strong feelings expressed by a man of the faith.
I now wish to deal for a few moments with a speech which was made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp). I do not want you to remind me about relevancy, Mr. Speaker, because I intend to be as relevant as the man to whom I am making reference at the moment, and I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that if the Minister of Trade and Commerce was not as politically blind and partisan, with the attitude of a bureaucrat-
Oh.

He did, you must agree, refuse to fulfil his responsibilities as a deputy minister because of political partisanship. He resigned not only because he could not get along with his staff but because his staff did not particularly care for him. The only way in which he could vindicate his honour was to get elected to this parliament where he could again display his bureaucratic arrogance. But he is not going to get away with it.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce made a speech to this house on the subamendment and his total disregard for relevancy only indicated to me that he is completely ignorant of the moral, political, cultural and historic aspects of the question involved. He showed no concern about any of these aspects. His concern was merely: How best do I advance the Liberal party?
Out of order completely.
What, the Liberal party?

The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that while Quebec Conservatives sat on their hands-or, rather, I will quote from the article before me. It says:
While Quebec Conservatives sat on their hands, Mr. Sharp asked the opposition lor the source of Mr. Diefenbaker's idea to modify the red ensign by the inclusion of a fleur-de-lis. He called it "a clumsy and gratuitous piece of appeasement- a bone thrown out to a troublesome minority."
These are his own words. Neither the Conservative party in this house nor any member of that party has ever used in reference to the French speaking Canadians of this

country, the words "troublesome minority". The words were uttered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and they are disgusting for a minister of the crown to use with that bureaucratic attitude of his.
As I was going through some of the interesting clippings I have in my possession I noticed another article bringing to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce the fact that he would not be able to get away with this partisan political attitude of his. This newspaper article reminds him that the arrogance of the Liberals helped to defeat them in 1957. Mr. Sharp, it says, revealed that it is one of the best Conservative assets today. How right he is.
In conclusion, I want to deal with one or two other aspects of this subject. I want to deal with the question of copyright as it affects the new flag. If the Prime Minister were to agree to a referendum, would parliament have the right to turn this matter over to the returning officers and ask them to include this design on the ballot during an election before the copyright has been cleared? I ask this because there was an article which appeared in the press very recently which I found most interesting, although I do not agree with some of the views which were expressed. The writer, Mr. Charles Lynch, said:
One of the unresolved problems confronting the government over the maple leaf flag is getting the design copyrighted.
When Prime Minister Pearson sent to the patent and copyright division here last week to find how many maple leaf copyrights there were he was told that 327 commercial firms hold a copyright on the maple leaf and 24 others have a copyright on three leaves.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to you that the course of action that would have to be taken by the federal government would be tantamount to the expropriation of a copyright. If this were the course of action taken in fact, I suppose that attitude on the part of the government would be no different from the attitude of the government in any "red" country, if you like.
It is not too many months ago, sir, that I read an article dealing with brand names and copyrights and how the cancellation of these copyrights affects business. My wife probably buys the majority of her meats and meat products from Canada Packers under the "Maple Leaf" label, but I am wondering if she could tell me who manufactures that particular brand. This was the concern of the advertising people, that literally thousands of women buy, not only food, not only

clothing but all sorts of household commodities daily and identify the product by the copyrighted name. The minister is looking at me; I see that he agrees with me wholeheartedly. What, then, happens to Canada Packers copyright; a name they have maintained with a degree of dignity for years and years-"Canada Packers Maple Leaf" products?
