This house has been discussing since the middle of June the resolution introduced by the government, for the adoption of a distinctive Canadian flag.
As early as January 27, 1960, when he was leader of the opposition, the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson) stated clearly the position of the Liberal party on this flag question. At that time, he proposed

Canadian Flag
to the then Conservative government to put before parliament legislation which, and I quote:
-if it were adopted by the representatives of the people, would settle the Issue of our national flag; parliament would then agree to adopt a distinctive flag which, unlike the red ensign to which parliament has never given official recognition, could not be mistaken for the flag of the United Kingdom or some colonies and could be easily identified as the Canadian flag.
Is it not consistent that now that he has become the leader of the Canadian government, the right hon. Prime Minister should propose a resolution in order to give Canada a distinctive national flag?
Like many other members, the right hon. Prime Minister received a number of letters from people complaining about measures that might be taken to replace the red ensign. The Prime Minister answered to those bona fide correspondents that he wanted to assure them of his unqualified respect for the union jack and the red ensign and for all they represent of our history and traditions as symbols of freedom and democracy. Nevertheless, it is time that Canada should be given a distinctive flag which would have the top position on the mast.
Canada has been waiting for a flag long enough. I am both happy and proud to see that the government has now seen fit to take steps in that direction. Our confederation will soon be a hundred years old. Discussions on the flag have been going on for years, right from the very beginning of our confederation, and until now it has always seemed that no agreement was possible. Will any further delay in finally adopting a national flag make for better understanding?
With the coming of the centennial and the world fair, there are other reasons besides the basic ones for adopting a distinctive flag now. There is the matter of convenience which should not be minimized.
Indeed, it is inconceivable that this country could welcome millions of visitors to those great events without being able to fly a flag unmistakably its own.
Since every country has its flag, why should Canada be an exception? The flag is actually a factor of national unity, in peacetime as well as in wartime. If other proposed flags are controversial, it is all the more necessary to cast them aside and start anew with a new emblem.
Now, the other flags mentioned, which were not approved officially but only tolerated, give rise to controversy. Therefore, they should be discarded as distinctive flags. As a country,

Canada takes part in all important international conferences. It is a middle power, but with bright prospects for future development in every respect. And such a country would be without a distinctive flag? You will admit that this is paradoxical.
Former generations were cautious on this subject. They did not jeopardize the future. The government is now convinced that Canada should have its own flag and it gives praise to the previous leaders who, in their wisdom, refrained from tying its hands in this connection.
The time has come for Canada to choose a permanent distinctive flag that will be kept by future generations since it will have been given a "clear" and official status.
All the present differences will be forgotten if this house puts aside narrow considerations and sectional interests to take the proper decision which is quite simple, that of giving the country an emblem which will be respected both at home and abroad, an emblem that will confirm the good reputation our country enjoys throughout the world, as travellers back from Europe, Asia and Africa can testify.
It has been said that the flag issue was liable to create emotional rather than rational reactions. Mr. Speaker, if the flag issue can give rise to purely emotional reactions, it can also be objectively dealt with as any other problem. It is up to us, as members of parliament, to be rational. Now, to give the country a distinctive flag for reasons of convenience, especially to consolidate unity among Canadians, is not an emotional but a rational issue.
Regardless of the emblem selected, there will undoubtedly be few but vocal reactionaries and disgruntled people. It is not possible to satisfy everybody. Considering the information gathered by the members of the house as a whole and after thinking the matter over and listening to a debate which has been going on for several weeks, I am firmly convinced that the people of the ten provinces want a distinctive flag.
I think that an autonomous country such as Canada has been since the Statute of Westminster has to adopt a flag whose design will not be reminiscent of any other country. Why should the country's emblem include reminders of Canada's ties with England and not with France? On the other hand, if we were to adopt a flag representing the two former hegemonies, ' it would be necessary to load the flag with complicated symbols and it would still not satisfy anyone. It is better to eliminate the symbols recalling France or

England and thus not only prevent differences ot opinion from continuing unabated but also prevent the new flag from becoming unacceptable to new Canadians who make up a large percentage of our population.
Thus we would have a common flag for the whole population, a flag which would not perpetuate the old quarrels we want to forget, which is a great advantage. The inclusion of symbols representing the motherlands would only feed old grudges. The adoption of a distinctive flag seems to be the only sound way to put an end to useless discussions on that issue.
The three maple leaves, the central element of the proposed flag, seem a logical choice since they represent Canada. Many pages of our literature, in both French and English, are devoted to the maple leaf. They contain many references to the maple tree which is quite representative of our country not because it is exclusive to Canada but because, due to its profusion and beauty, its praises have been sung by Canadian poets and lyrics writers.
Hon. members should not prolong this debate unnecessarily by lengthy discussions of details. That is why I prefer to stick with a distinctive flag containing three maple leaves rather than risk embroiling matters and putting off the selection of a distinctive flag indefinitely.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra said in the house, on June 30 last:
I believe Canada needs not only a distinctive flag but a distinctive Canadian spirit.
That distinctive spirit should be embodied in a flag whose judicial status is well established. It should represent all Canadians and, in my opinion, the three maple leaves flag should be the national flag of Canada and should prevail over all those which we had in the past.
The point here is not to please French Canadians any more than others, as suggested in certain narrow-minded political quarters. But if we take a look at history, we must admit that French Canadians have special reasons to favour the maple leaf flag, having been pioneers in the development of the west as well as the east, through their daring explorers and missionaries, laymen and clerics as well.
English speaking people of good will could not, any more than French Canadians, repudiate the distinctive flag proposed. Canada is the common country of the descendants of French and English pioneers. It has become gradually the country of immigrants of all nationalities who chose to come here 20220-462-J
Canadian Flag
to start a new life that had become impossible for them in their country of origin and gave Canada the best of their talents and industry. No one among those three groups should stand against the adoption of a flag which is long overdue. On the contrary, everyone should look forward with enthusiasm to the day when it will fly on high in the Canadian sky.

Mr. Speaker, this is my first intervention in the debate. I have had my name on the list of speakers for some time, but the list is long and it takes quite a while before one's name is reached. It is a pleasure to follow my hon. friend, the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), and I hope that the remarks I have to make although somewhat different, will be along the same lines of Canadianism that he has envisaged.
I have noticed that many members who have spoken in beginning their remarks have made personal references to their own backgrounds and the backgrounds of their constituencies, and I want to do the same. Many hon. members have referred to service in the first and second world wars and their association with the red ensign. I think I am one of the few, if not the only one in the house, who can say that my entire career at sea during the second world war, a very inauspicious career I might add, was spent serving under the red ensign. Those of us in the merchant navy, however, grew to honour and appreciate the old red duster.
For the record, I think hon. members will find that the red ensign was first officially used on British mercantile ships in 1707 and has been used ever since. The first instance in Canada of the use of the red ensign with the dominion badge or seal added was in 1892.
May I also refer to Saint John and make some brief remarks about this historic city. Many hon. members will, of course, associate Saint John with the Loyalists. We are very proud of our Loyalist tradition and it is becoming a greater source of pride every day. I think I should point out that for a considerable period of its history Saint John was under the French flag, a similar period to that when Annapolis Royal was under French rule, as referred to by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) the other day. Many people do not know this.
I recall that when a measure was introduced in the house in 1954 concerning historic sites the then minister of northern affairs, now premier of Quebec, did not realize this fact

Canadian Flag
and promised consideration when I mentioned that here was a very good example of two eras of colonial control in a city. The Fort LaTour period to which I am referring extended from 1631 to 1645 and it was the first major French outpost in New Brunswick. Prior to that time there were two earlier phases of Indian life. The story of the first English settlement on the Saint John river more than a century after the LaTour-D'Aulnay struggle between two rival French traders is recalled by the well known trading posts associated with the Simonds, Hazen and White period. Thus, at Portland point in Saint John are significant historical phases in the lives of three racial strains, Indians, French and English. Each has played an important role in the history of our province. When to these are added the famous Loyalist settlement one has a good idea of the different strains in our city and province.
I think it is important to understand why the Loyalists came to New Brunswick. They were a unique group comprising many well educated men and certainly men of great principle. Not nearly enough credit has been given in our history books to these gallant exiles. Some have suggested that had they found in their midst in the United States a true leader such as George Washington they might have remained there and brought about a different course of history. But they did not hesitate. They brought with them their valuable possessions, their education and culture, but above all else their love of a monarchical form of government. They were not interested in republicanism in any form. That is why in New Brunswick and Saint John we have such a pleasant mixture of culture from which many can take a lesson. We have a pleasant blend of American heritage with a true love for the crown, not a blind obedience but an appreciation of the monarchy as a better form of government than a republic.
It is important to define what one means by "imperialism" and I go to the work, "Canadians In The Making", by Professor A. R. M. Lower. On page 349 he states:
Canadian imperialism has never been simple: it can at one and the same time be bitterly contemptuous of Englishmen and warmly welcome the British connection. A newspaper in that most loyal of all Canadian cities, Saint John, could write, apropos of a book by an English traveller: "Canadians might never suspect how coarse, ignorant, conceited and, withal, amusing they are if talented Englishmen did not come out occasionally and write books about them." Imperialism was in its own way a kind of Canadian nationalism.
In supporting the subamendment put forward by Ihe hon. member for Regina City

(Mr. More) I want to say at the beginning that I feel a subject such as the flag should not have been brought up for debate in the house. I liken it to capital punishment. It is a very emotional subject. People take positions for different reasons and it is extremely difficult to get a truly free vote on such a subject. In addition, of course, bitter controversy enters the picture.
However, we are involved in a historic debate to which many good contributions have been made. I do not wish to single out any but I think that speeches both inside and outside the house have been worthy of commendation on all sides. I noticed that last night the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. McLean), a good friend of mine, made a contribution to the debate, and I give him credit for doing so. I do not agree with his thoughts. I think it must have been extremely difficult for him to make that speech. He is a member of the Royal Canadian Legion, active in the boy scouts, a veteran of the first world war and is of Scottish ancestry. His riding is almost completely associated with the British tradition. Yet he came out in favour of the new flag which, of course, means scrapping the red ensign.
I have always been interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) about a republic. I find it difficult to believe there is support for a republic in his riding and I can only say he is either foolhardy or he knows what his people are thinking. It strikes me that in a historic place like Lotbiniere the people would certainly have great respect for the monarchical form of government.
I was also interested in the speech of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) the other day. Everybody in the house knows he is a very active Anglican layman, and I say more power to him. But in his speech he disowned completely the red ensign and its historic traditions and connections with the Anglican church. He made absolutely no reference to it. I am not criticizing his stand but I think he should have tried to explain this change in his thinking.
We have also had, of course, the famous speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) which has been given so much attention. I can only say that it represented a walking of the plank such as we have not seen since the days of Captain Bligh. Hon. members may ask when I think the flag crisis became serious, and I should like to go back to the 1940's for a moment. I lay the entire blame on the Liberal party

and their failure to provide proper, enlightened national leadership, particularly during the so-called Mackenzie King era. I say that they have failed even to grasp the essentials of nationhood and I intend to prove this point.
In his speech the other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce showed great solicitude for the future and fortunes of the Conservative party. I intend to demonstrate it is his type of membership in the so-called Ottawa establishment of liberal, with a small "1", civil servants, English speaking and British educated in most cases, which is more to blame than anything else for the division that has crept into the country. I intend to show that this group who typify this pseudo-Canadianism, and I include in it the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) and any other members of this Ottawa hierarchy, willy-nilly accepted the Mackenzie King philosophy of the day, this misguided Liberalism of the first water that played with the constitution and turned our national life into the volcano of power politics to sustain at all costs the life of the Liberal party. These individuals were the henchmen, knowingly or otherwise who perpetuated the legacy of William Lyon Mackenzie King. The victims, Mr. Speaker, are you and I, the Canadian people, and we are paying for it dearly today in many ways, particularly in the departure of many of our symbols and traditions that go to the very root of our way of life?
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
How do you reconcile your words this afternoon with your party's slogan in the 1957-58 election campaign, "Canada first"? Is there an apple gone bad over there?

Well, I intend to demonstrate that the Conservative party has put Canada first, but not at all costs like the Liberals under Mackenzie King.
The flag, while it may give the foundation of our traditions is only an outward symbol. This deliberate policy of tampering with the distinctive emblems of our past history can only result in the weakening of the monarchy and, of course, our nationhood. The creeping republicanism that has been challenged so forcefully by Dr. Eugene Forsey can
Canadian Flag
only result in turning this nation to republicanism. I wish to quote for a moment from Dr. Eugene Forsey's remarks which were made in 1955 in a radio broadcast on January 14. They show his foresightedness and they demonstrate the beginnings of the problems that you and I have to face. I quote his remarks:
But why do I call all this "creeping republicanism?" Well, "creeping" it most certainly is; sly, slithering, serpentine. And I just wish I had time to recite to you the bad history, bad law, bad logic, the insults, the crass ignorance, the distortions of the dictionary, with which the government and its hangers-on have tried to defend the indefensible. They are almost beyond belief.
It's creeping and it's "republicanism." It just doesn't make sense on any other basis. If it was all innocent, why the long years of stealth and secrecy? Why the flouting of law and constitution? Somebody has had some serious purpose in all this. It may not have been the government itself. Ministers may have just yielded to pressure. But, inside the government or outside, or both, the pressure has been there, steady, insistent, relentless. The people who applied it knew what they wanted; to root out familiar and distinctive terms which bind us to our institutions, so that they could remould them nearer to their hearts' desire. They would never have got as far as they have if more of us realized what the monarchy meant, and why it was worth preserving. But, that's another story: the melancholy story of how, for nearly 30 years, our people have been steadily and systematically miseducated about our constitution, and particularly about the role of the crown as the guardian of that constitution, the protector of parliament and the people against cabinet dictatorship. Fortunately, however, there have been many thousands who have never bowed the knee unto Baal; and there are signs now that many thousands more are beginning to understand what has been happening, and to resist. That resistance will spell the end of "creeping republicanism."
I mention that to show that the policy of Mackenzie King has been continued by his successors in the Liberal party. The Liberals, at times in our history, played an important part, but not as great a part as the party of which I am a member. They have played their share in our formative years, but someone forgot to tell them to stop.
Having blamed this creeping republicanism on Mackenzie King, it is only fair to ask why these changes were allowed to take place. Why is it that everything connected with our English background has to be removed? I refer not only to the designation of "dominion" which was removed from our telephone books, but even the word "royal" has been removed from the phrase "royal mail" on post office boxes. Even the word "British" itself now brings hatred and anger in some quarters. In my opinion, it is all the fault of incorrect premises, the assumptions centred around Quebec and our French traditions. In

Canadian Flag
order to obtain Canadian unity we must accept French Canada as the basic, positive form of Canadianism, and English speaking Canadians must work to become identified with this type of true Canada. In other words, it seems to have become an established fact that no Canadian virtues are to be found in our Anglo-Saxon traditions.
As a witness, I call a book entitled "Freedom Wears a Crown" by John Farthing. This was an outstanding young Canadian who died at an early age. Like Dr. Forsey, he foresaw what was happening. I predict that as the years go by this will become a very famous book. This is what he said on page 87 of this book:
It is of the essence of the Kingsian conception of Canadian unity, not only that such unity is to involve an harmonious relationship between the French and the English communities in this country, but that harmony is possible only by destroying all real sense of community among the English speaking people of Canada. They must find themselves as a people by ceasing to mean or to stand for anything in and of themselves, save what is compatible with a unity the terms of which are dictated by others. The English speaking people of Canada are to find unity and hence their soul by standing ready to relinquish every shred of their heritage and tradition, and to abandon everything that has hitherto given them a distinctive character and made them the not wholly contemptible people that they are.
Although I have made a great many references to Quebec, I feel it is English Canada and many of the leaders mentioned who bear a greater responsibility. If there have been meaningful contributions by English Canada, then they have been obscured. The leaders have failed and I charge the Liberal party with this neglect because, after all, they have governed this country certainly for a majority of years in recent times. It is not the fault of Quebec, let there be no mistake about it-* it is not the fault of Quebec that no one knows what English Canada is doing. We do not know our own achievements, our goals and our frontiers. While I do not pretend to know what French Canadians want or where they are going, I am certain we English Canadians have lost sight of our objectives, of our culture and nationalism.
It may be also that Anglo-Saxon Canadianism has been too apologetic and too negative. It may be that we have advanced economically, but other movements have been stifled. This is why I am attempting to lay the cards on the table. We may not need a silent revolution, as is the case in Quebec now, but we do need a different type of Canada, one that espouses certain basic terms, not of one Canada or the other but in the traditions of

each. I want to say that the leader of my party consistently, throughout the years, has stood for one Canada.
Having said this, Mr. Speaker, I quote once more from this book "Freedom Wears a Crown". Mr. Farthing has expressed this in a much better way than I could:
-the people of French Canada are faced with the same basic issue as are their English speaking compatriots. We have to decide whether we are to become again a democracy functioning according to our constitutional idea and ideal of government, or whether we are to become a dependant republic. That is the basic issue of Canadian unity and those are the terms in which the question has valid meaning. It is also the first and all important question facing Canada, since the answer to almost every other question will depend upon the answer we give to it. The question belongs outside partisan power-plays. It is a matter far too serious to be subjected to appeals to popular prejudice on either side. It ought to be treated in a manner befitting an adult people mature in their political thinking.
Having said that about certain matters of French and English Canadian nationalism, I now deal briefly with what has been referred to as republicanism. I do not know what degree of republicanism there is in this country today. The hon. member for Lot-biniere (Mr. Choquette) stood up in this house in answer to a question and said flatly he was a republican. He also said he was not a separatist. I find it very difficult to assess how a person could be a republican and not a separatist, but he has stated, as a member of parliament sitting in this house, that he is in favour of a republic. Evidently there must be some feeling for this in his constituency.
I call as my first witness a very distinguished French Canadian. I refer of course to Premier Jean Lesage of Quebec who, in the triumphant tour which we all recall he made of France in 1963, said in London, according to a dispatch in the Chronicle-Herald by Mr. Eric Dennis:
Premier Jean Lesage of Quebec said here yesterday that the flames of nationalism in his province, fired by "a feeling of resentment over not getting a square deal" in the Canadian partnership were now on the wane.
And at the same time he assured the British that "French Canadians as a whole looked to London and the crown as their great protector."
"The French Canadian would be the last to join the United States if there was any move for Canada to be absorbed by the Americans," he added. "He wants to stay in the commonwealth. The French Canadian is a royalist. Never forget that."
I place this on the record with pleasure. It shows the division between the federal and Quebec Liberals on this matter of a republic,

and it is also comforting to know that at least someone in Quebec is in favour of the monarchy.
As my last witness I recall the words of Lord Elgin who, in 1847, referring to the proper respect being shown at that time for French nationalism, asked:
Who will not venture to say the last hand which waves the British flag on American ground may not be that of a French Canadian?
The main criticism that has been made in this debate has been in reference to the timing, and this is still the unanswered question as the days roll on. Why was the flag issue introduced in the middle of a busy legislative program, a program that was slowly showing some success? Why was it that the Prime Minister all of a sudden interrupted the daily business of the _ house and introduced the flag debate? Was it that the Queen's visit had something to do with the Prime Minister's decision suddenly to stop the government's business that was, after all, making some progress?
One thing is certain, and I say this to the senior minister presently in the house, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), we cannot be debating a flag in this house when the Queen is inspecting troops outside on the lawn of parliament hill. This is my argument; it is difficult to separate the flag from the crown because exactly the same arguments apply.
We hear a great deal these days about being broadminded. I may be old fashioned but I think there is too much broadmindedness in the modern world. This may be one of the reasons why we parents are failing, as evidenced by the many problems of our juveniles. Perhaps we have failed in our responsibilities to the youth of this nation in not bringing forth a proper nationalism with the necessary symbols that demonstrate the great strength of our system of government which is, as I say, in monarchical form.
While we fear the extremism that is showing itself across the border, and has been particularly in evidence in recent days, it is surely not wrong to stand for something which demonstrates the essential character of this country and protects, constitutionally at least, all that is French Canadian. I refer of course to the main theme in my remarks today, the symbol of the crown.
Let us remember that we chose in Canada as our political system the monarchical form of government. For one, I would like to see the crown on our flag if the red ensign is not to be. I think this would be a protection for our commonwealth link and it would dem-
Canadian Flag
onstrate to all in this nation, particularly the youth, the system of government under which we live, and it would put the lie to all those who have false ideas of a republic.
We made our decision freely, both elements, the French and the English, that the crown, the cabinet and the Commons would be our constitutional form of government. We cannot abrogate any one of these three elements; and that is why I am extremely worried that any inroads on the crown, be it merely symbols or designations, or some serious change in the constitution itself, will drastically weaken our whole form of government.
To get back to my own position, I have stated at home and I repeat now that I strongly believe in the red ensign, or red ensign with modifications, and have for some time pledged my support to the Canadian Legion, the I.O.D.E. and the many other organizations that have argued for the retention of the red ensign as Canada's national flag. I do not know the thoughts of all those in the mari-times but I am certain that the majority favour the retention of the red ensign, but I put this qualification on the record that if in some way it could be proven that the new flag of the Prime Minister is a final act of Canadian unity then we might have different thoughts. But as I have said, to me this suggests other steps and I feel it has caused serious misgivings, and that is the reason why many are digging in.
However, if the majority of the Canadian people indicate by plebiscite or otherwise a preference for the Prime Minister's design, unhandsome as this design may be, or any other design, I would accept it and I am sure this would be the wish of my constituency. I would also support any reasonable compromise that would come forward-and I notice today many of the newspapers, such as the Montreal Gazette, are calling for such a compromise. This could give us an opportunity to return home and obtain a better assessment of the views of our electors.
If a committee of this house were set up, as was suggested by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) and later taken up by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) it would of course meet with my approval. We would be certain that by doing this an election would be avoided, and each of us could get down to the serious business of our country and make our long term plans for real unity in 1967 and the great future of Canada. There has been some criticism made of the type of debate. I took part in the pipe line debate a few years ago and at that time

Canadian Flag
we did not apologize for any of the parliamentary tactics which were used. I think the same holds true today, even though the issue has not at this stage reached the same proportions.
I again call as a witness in connection with this matter of parliamentary tactics Dr. Forsey who, in the course of an address to the men's and women's Canadian clubs on June 19, 1956, in Edmonton-the home city of the hon. member who preceded me and who made such an excellent speech in this debate-had this to say:
Construction is neither new nor vicious. It is, of course, "not by any to be taken in hand unadvisedly, lightly or wantonly, but reverently, discreetly, advisedly, soberly," and from a deep conviction that it is indispensable in the public interest. Obstruction is a legitimate, recognized, time-honoured and essential part of the parliamentary system; in the last resort, with the government's power of dissolution, the only way of keeping parliament responsible to the people.
In closing, I merely wish to say that we in the official opposition are taking our action in this flag matter "reverently, discreetly, advisedly and soberly".

Mr. Speaker, a flag is, and always has been, a symbol raised high, a focal point for those intense feelings of joy and grief, fear and faith, aspiration and courage felt both individually and shared simultaneously in a common and uniting experience.
The flag as a symbol has enfolded in memory for many people all the vivid colour of past deeply rooted experiences of national life. Sometimes it waves proudly on the stage of memory as an emblem of triumph and achievement; again, it may conceal crucial and painful events which some, understandably do not wish to relive. But whatever it means or does not mean to each of us in this place, we must all recognize the fact that for many it is deeply rooted in a sense of identity.
As a student, years ago, I remember a teacher suddenly directing a question to a fellow student: "How do you know who you are?" And the answer came: "Because I am the one who has had a certain set of experiences". We began to consider memory as a key to identity. The chain of experiences that contribute to identity are emotionally coloured and achieve importance in our lives depending on the intensity of their emotional content. The flag is bound by ties of emotion to some very important events in the lives of people.
In the course of our national history, this allegiance to a known and honoured flag has 
been-and especially has this been true in time of war-strongly encouraged by leaders and those who influence the lives of men.
If such a flag is suddenly lowered, emotions may flood forth whose intensity may well surprise both the individual and the nation. This is what we have seen happening before our very eyes during the past few weeks. More and more people have been realizing their close identification with a flag that is being torn aside, and feeling a sense of shock and loss of identity in the process. We must speak for these people. And the government must offer them something more than the assurance of its respect for their flag as a memory.
Some have said: "What is a flag? A flag is only what we make of it". This is true. This is what has happened down through the years with the red ensign. People have attached to it very deep emotional significance, the intensity of which was not always consciously realized. But when that symbol is threatened, the area of threat widens and deepens to arouse emotions that might well have slumbered, and we discover that it is no light thing to tamper with what lies deep within the hearts and minds of people.
One cannot sit in judgment, for who of us can judge? There is not one who does not have deep emotional and idealistic ties which involve objects and associated beliefs and circumstances; the flag is a prime example of this kind of attachment.
I am going to read some extensive comments from one letter I received from a constituent on this subject-a veteran of world war two. These are very interesting and thoughtful comments from an individual who plays a responsible role in the community, and who says:
I am against the new flag. I am not violently against it at the moment, and yet my feelings are strange-it does not necessarily mean I am easy about it, nor that anybody can do anything they want. It is unsettling to feel that somebody can come along and interfere with it, pass a resolution and give us a new one. I wouldn't want to fight over it. And yet I don't want anybody else doing anything to change it. I think many people out here feel the same way.
Then the writer goes on:
I feel they weighed this flag business on votes, not on the roots of the country or the sensibilities and deep loyalties of the people. When I see the red ensign, I don't think of Britain, I think of Canada. When somebody suggests getting rid of it I also see St. Andrew's cross in that flag, and I'm sure others see St. Patrick's cross and the cross of St. George. People say "Of course, your support of the red ensign is an emotional thing". If support for the flag we have is an emotional argument, then is it not also an emotional argument to attack it or suggest removal of it? If

emotion is to be ruled out, then the emotions of the other side must be ruled out also.
Certainly it is an emotional thing. Canadians are not too demonstrative. We make use of our flag as much as we do, I think, because Americans are such flag wavers they forced us into it.
We are embarrassed when we sing O Canada or The Queen, but let nobody for a moment think we do not feel emotions about such things.
The flag does not determine the nation; the nation determines the flag. If Canada had used another symbol at Vimy Ridge, if another symbol had flown from her ships, airports and army depots during the second world war; if it had fluttered over our men in Hong Kong, Dieppe, Sicily, Or-tona, on D-day; if our soldiers, sailors and airmen had been buried under it during the second world war, then we could all be proud of that flag.
No. Canada made the red ensign what it is today. Must we pitch over many years of work and sacrifice now?
He goes on:
Is a flag something that from time to time we invite an interior decorator in to have changed, to be brought up to date? No, it's not. Canada has many years of tradition invested in the red ensign and this must not be lightly discarded as we would an old sofa.
Is a commercial artist to choose our flag? Or is it not proper to let those who have sacrificed most keep the one they served under and would serve again?
He goes on:
Parliament must tread with care. There is still ample reason for feeling that men are moved today by certain honoured symbols just as they were moved in the days of the pipes and the claymore and the battle cry.
The idea boys would have nothing to do with this sort of factor; it's not scientific; it's not logical. But they are not dealing with chemicals, computers or statistics; they are dealing with human beings.
That is why our flag should not be controversial. It is above that; just as it is above our heads as it flies from thousands of slender poles throughout the country today.
Mr. Speaker, many members have very seriously and ably presented arguments to justify retention of the red ensign either as it is or in modified form. May I say, with all respect, I believe these arguments are not essential to the present situation, because the central fact remains that millions of Canadian people are not yet ready to give it up. That fact in itself, in a democratic country, should be sufficient reason to give the government pause and inspire it to pursue a different course.
Hear, hear.

We are not really concerned with justification for allegiance so much as we are concerned with our clear duty to recognize and respect the reality of a continuing loyalty to a flag that signifies so much to so many.
Canadian Flag
Surely this capacity to accept and deal with a situation as it develops is one that is not foreign to politicians and governments. It is an important aspect of political life. One cannot say, "This should not be". The fact is, it is; this is the situation-and from the point of view of democracy it has to be dealt with in the light of what course is best for the Canadian people. And the voice of the people must be heard. I hope that even before consideration is given, for example, in the form of a plebiscite as outlined by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More) there would be a decision made by the Prime Minister to refer this far reaching and troublesome question to a committee not subject to a time limit; for to invite speed here is to summon discord.
This place is not a show, and those who impatiently watch the deliberations in this chamber must not expect a glib and arbitrary disposal of problems which would slur over the rights and expressed desires of millions of Canadian people.
Hear, hear.

On this important question of a flag for Canada, the onus is on the government to adopt a different course, a course in the direction of mutual respect and harmony; and on this path may discretion be the better part of valour.

Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in rising, as the spokesman of the people in my riding of Nicolet-Yamaska on the matter of a distinctive national flag.
As far as I am concerned, I am exerting the privilege loaned by the people of Nicolet-Yamaska-and I say loaned because the people of my constituency can at any time take away this privilege I have the right of exerting today-that is to be able to rise in the house as often as I want to express my views in all due freedom of speech and action.
At this time, the opposition is blamed without rhyme or reason for staging a filibuster on the question of a distinctive national flag. For the time being, the people, more particularly in the province of Quebec, believe that this discussion has already lasted four months. No, Mr. Speaker, this debate has not lasted so long as that, for we have hardly had 15 days of discussion.
I believe that I expressed my views on various occasions on the flag, and I have still not changed my mind, when I state that I am in favour of a distinctive national flag for Canada.

Canadian Flag
Hear, hear.

On November 21, 1962, I mentioned in the house what I believed to be the five points we should consider before choosing a distinctive design which could be flown throughout Canada, in every province, and would also represent Canada in every country in the world.
The policy of the Conservative party is well known in this respect, and last Thursday, I was proud to hear the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), whom I have always admired-perhaps because I am particularly devoted to the cause of our farmers -tell the house which principles the Conservative party wants to see preserved when a distinctive national flag is chosen. First of all, he said that the flag should be acceptable to the majority of Canadians. Second, it should recognize our dual culture and be a symbol of our history. Third, the flag should have a religious significance. Fourth, Canada's political evolution should be accepted without revolution.
In 1962, I said first that I wanted this debate, which holds the attention of the Canadian nation, to be carried on with dignity and not to be made into a matter of political partisanship.
By the way, I would like to tell my colleagues who sit in this house that we must now discuss this matter and that when it has been decided, those who have not spoken should not range all over Canada and pit one race against the other, as has often been done in the past, and more especially in our province, when for 30 or 40 years we have heard about conscription and heard charges to the effect that a political party was in favour of conscription or war. If we do not want to play one race against the other, we must say immediately what we have to say, listen to the viewpoints of others and then walk hand in hand towards the ideal that we have set up.
If this first point is to be efficient, all political partisanship must be eliminated, so that the flag design which the nation will choose will be selected not by a single man but by a group representing all political parties, a group which has no reason to indulge in political partisanship by suggesting such and such a choice. That was the first point I mentioned in November 1962.
The second point I raised was the following: if all Canadians recognize the necessity of having a flag of their own, on the other hand they do not all agree on the flag design. All members are aware of that and

they have received through the mails hundreds of designs for a distinctive national flag. But all do not agree on the design and that is why the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) moved an amendment to the resolution and the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More) introduced a subamendment. By the amendment and subamendment, they ask the government to let the people decide the flag design. I shall revert to this question in a few moments.
The third point was the following: I am not one of those who want to ram a flag design down the throat of the rest of the nation. I agree that each group should try and have the rest of the nation understand that such and such design should be chosen.
At the present time we are discussing a design proposed by one man and consisting of three red maple leaves on a white field with two blue bands at each end. That design was chosen, as I said, by one man or by a small group without any previous discussion, not even at the caucus of the party involved or in the cabinet.
That design was chosen and they want to give it to the Canadian people. But when someone objects or gives his views on the design chosen, he is charged with being against a distinctive national flag. As far as I am concerned I do not like the design with the three red maple leaves, but I am for a distinctive national flag. I do not like this design, like several of my compatriots in the province of Quebec.
At this stage, Mr. Speaker, I should like to report a fact that happened in my home. When I arrived with copies of the flag with three maple leaves on a white shield and blue bands, my ten year old son asked me: "What is this?" I said: "This is the flag proposed by the government in the House of Commons." Then, he asked me: "What are those three things in the centre?" I told him: "Those are maple leaves." He answered: "Dad, we have maples on our farm. We have some in the yard and the leaves do not look like these. They are not the maple leaves we see here, in our yard, on our farm."
Honestly, Mr. Speaker, I admit that the remarks of that young boy saying they were not maple leaves made me think twice.
And they would like to adopt a flag, telling the Canadian people that those are maple leaves.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Certainly.
Does the hon. member think that the fleur-de-lis represented on the flag of the province of Quebec look like those he sees in his garden?

Mr. Speaker, to answer the
minister, I shall say that, before I was elected as a member of the House of Commons, I did not think that a minister could be like the hon. member for St. Jean-Iber-ville-Napierville.
Answer my question-
I thought a minister was quite different.
I asked you a very simple question. Answer it.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, surely the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis) had no right to get up in the house without recognition from you and interfere with the speech of the hon. member.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps I should mention to the hon. member that I have recognized the minister. I think the Chair can recognize an hon. member otherwise than by standing and calling on him by naming his constituency or his cabinet position. The minister got up and asked permission to ask a question, and this was granted by the hon. member who has the floor. I suggest that that was tantamount to recognition.

Mr. Speaker, my fourth point is this. A Canadian flag is a symbol of unity; it should not divide a nation. Now, when we have reached a compromise enabling us to choose a really distinctive Canadian flag, we can rest assured that it will be flown with pride in every Canadian province, including the province of Quebec, and honoured by the whole Canadian nation.
That is what I said in 1962 and what I am saying again today.
We must select a design which will unite and not divide the nation. We must choose a design which will be a rallying sign.
If we could decide upon such a choice, I, for one, think that it would be to the greatest advantage of all Canadians in every province of Canada.
My fifth point is this. I should like to point out once again that our flag should be a symbol of unity. Bearing that in mind, our flag should be so designed that it takes into account the aspirations of the two main groups
Canadian Flag
in the country. It should reflect our sovereignty, our accession to the rank of independent state and show that we are free from any political link of subservience.
There is now in Canada a nation-wide group which cannot conceive a Canadian flag without the union jack being an integral part of it. There is another group on the government side which cannot conceive that Canada can have a distinctive flag without retaining the union jack as a second flag.
Therefore, as far as I am concerned, I feel that exactly the same question is now being discussed. Several, maybe all of my English speaking friends, attach prime importance to the union jack. A few want it on the new flag and others want it as second flag.
Would it not be possible to have, maybe not the union jack, but something that would represent it, for our English speaking fellow citizens?
When the Leader of the Opposition proposed some amendments to the flag Canada recognized by order in council in 1945, by including a fleur-de-lis, he did not want to appease French Canadians as suggested unadvisedly, in my opinion, by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, when he stated:
A clumsy and gratuitous piece of appeasement: it must have appeared to my French Canadian friends as a bone thrown out to a troublesome minority to keep them quiet.
Frankly, I do not believe that in proposing
that a fleur-de-lis be added to a flag design, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition ever wanted to appease thereby the French speaking Canadians. He wanted to find a compromise, so that the two great founding races of this country could be represented on the same flag. He was looking for some common ground where, together, we could unite under the same flag.
Personally, I object to the union jack, in its present form, being shown on the distinctive flag. I want what the people of my riding want. I object also-and I speak honestly-to the fleur-de-lis being shown on the distinctive flag. But I might accept on the flag what the union jack means for my English-speaking friends and what the fleur-de-lis means for my French speaking friends. I would also accept on the distinctive flag symbols of our ties with our mother countries. Mr. Speaker, because of this proposal, I would not like my friends in the Liberal party to say or claim that I am throwing a bone to my English speaking friends.
For instance, if we could go back to the origin of our two races, we would find that

Canadian Flag
in 1497 John Cabot came to Canada, more exactly to Newfoundland, under a royal mandate, flying the white banner with St. George's cross. Later on, when Jacques Cartier came and discovered Canada in 1534, he flew a blue pennant with a white cross. Each having a royal warrant, those two men came to discover this country, and this was the starting point of a great nation.
If we were able to take those two crosses representing the English and French flags, and place them on a white field symbolizing the vast snowfields of this country, the Indians and Eskimos, in short, if we could arrange those two crosses without giving either of them priority, to show that this is a union of two great races which we formed in this country, and that we propose to go on working for its prosperity, we should certainly obtain the support of all our people.
The union of those two races would form a circle, which is the sign of unity, and we would, because of those two crosses, obtain the colours of Canada: blue, white and red.
On this flag, we would have a cross, which is the sign of a Christian nation. As 97 or perhaps 98 per cent of Canadian citizens are Christians, I do not think that a cross on a flag could be dishonourable; on the contrary, I think that a cross on the flag would certainly honour the Canadian nation. In the central circle, there could be a green maple leaf, which would indicate a growing Canada. That maple leaf might have 10 points, because an ordinary maple leaf can have 9, 10, 11 and even 12 points. Those 10 points would represent the ten Canadian provinces, and if, later on, another province happened to join the big Canadian family, another point might simply be added, to identify the new province.
Such a flag would have neither union jack nor fleur-de-lis, but it would indicate what the union jack means to a great number of our English speaking friends.
We would have the white cross on a field of azure to remind us of our past and we would have a circle in the middle to indicate that we are a united people in a country represented by a green maple leaf.
We could then visit our schools and meet the students. We could explain to them the meaning of the flag by recalling the whole Canadian history. We could start with 1497, mention 1534 and go on to confederation in 1867. We could tell them about the confederation pact and finally we would say: We are a united people.

In my opinion, this flag would be first and foremost a flag accepted by the majority of Canadians. Moreover, it would recognize our dual culture and would symbolize our history. It would also have a religious significance and would acknowledge the political evolution of Canada, without being revolutionary.

Mr. Speaker, having not heard the question I cannot answer it.
Once more, I wish to repeat this: at the present time, there are in the Liberal party members who will not speak on this flag issue. They will not speak on the second part of the resolution either.
I wish to tell them this: it would be much preferable that you say what you have to say here, in the house, instead of making all kinds of statements in the province of Quebec during the next federal election, in order to set one part of the population against the other.
I mention that, Mr. Speaker, because we meet at the present time organizers and members of that party who ask us, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce did the other day: What are you going to do to get elected in the province of Quebec, if you are against the three maple leaf flag?
But that does not mean that we are against a distinctive flag. And I would tell them this: It is not by flying a flag that all the problems we are confronted with at the present time in the province of Quebec will be settled. For 30 years, it paid dividends, for instance, to talk about conscription, but now, the farmers and the labourers want the country to look towards economy and not only towards emotion.
I even invited a group of members to spend a week in my constituency during the next election and to speak about the flag. Meanwhile, since my electors know my opinion on this matter, I shall speak about other things of greater importance.
What is happening in the province of Quebec is precisely that people realize that for too long, in the federal parliament, we discussed emotional matters only to do windowdressing and we forgot to discharge our responsibilities concerning economic matters.
I should like to quote from memory a speech made by Hon. Arthur Sauve, former federal minister, father of the late Paul Sauve, premier of the province of Quebec. Speaking at the college of L'Assomption, in 1931 or 1932, he said: "If we want to discuss politics

in the province of Quebec, we must appeal to emotions-that is what the Liberals were doing at that time-while in other provinces, we must discuss politics and bring forth arguments."
Well, I believe that is a thing of the past in the province of Quebec as in other provinces. If we wish to discuss politics, let us use arguments and stop appealing to emotions and tell

"Because you are against the three-leaved flag, even if you are in favour of a distinctive flag, you shall go down to defeat at the next election."
As far as I am concerned, I am and will always remain in favour of a distinctive national flag. I would be glad if, at last, the right hon. Prime Minister of this country would decide to convene a committee of the house. We would discuss the matter for a few weeks and I am sure we would be able to choose a design acceptable to all Canadians, or at least to the great majority of them.
If the committee is convened, I personally will propose the design I mentioned earlier, in order that all the members of the house may realize that by retaining what symbolizes the past of each race, we will have a flag which will unify the two groups and bring them closer together, in short, which will not divide them.
Moreover, if, as a last resort, I have to fight to have the three maple leaves replaced by one, as seen on this flag, especially of a colour which stands for a growing Canada, a united Canada, perhaps made up of two races-not only perhaps, but actually composed of two distinct races forming a great Canada, a complete whole-well, I shall fight to have those three maple leaves replaced by one maple leaf only.
If it is impossible for us, in this house, to make the Prime Minister understand that his three red maple leaf flag will not be readily accepted among the Canadian people, we should be able to make him realize that it is not enough to come and tell the people: "Here is a distinctive flag, do not bother about the design", because, once the people have the flag accepted and raised it, it will be too late to say, after a year or two: "Well, we should have had this or that on the flag instead of those three maple leaves". We must then accept it as is and never change it.
That is why we are exerting so much pressure and making these requests. We beg our colleagues of the Liberal party to exert pressure on the Prime Minister to set up a committee to choose a design which, as I said, would unite and not divide the country,

in short, knit together into one unit all the elements of our country.
I am sure that my English speaking friends are prepared to make major concessions and that they are prepared, as I said earlier, while retaining what, for them, symbolizes their past and their origin, to find a design that will satisfy both groups and still be accepted by the majority of Canadians.
